kp.k: Fixed-backend experiment compares three coding interfaces
kp.d: Fan, Liu, Pan and Zhang report a study of 60 professional software engineers and advanced computer science students: 36 used Inline, Chat and Structured interfaces across three counterbalanced Python tasks; 24 completed the same tasks without AI. All AI modes used GPT-4o, version 2024-11-20, with fixed decoding and no tools or web access. The tasks covered parsing, authentication debugging and batch REST requests. This is evidence about AI-assisted programming, not a direct study of legal work.

kp.k: AI improves immediate workload, speed and correctness
kp.d: Pooled AI assistance reduced the study's four-subscale RAW–TLX workload composite by 18.2 points on a 0–100 scale, with 95% CI [−22.3, −14.0]. Completion time was 25.0 versus 32.1 minutes, a time ratio of 0.78 [0.74, 0.83]. Correctness improved from an estimated 6.2/10 to 7.6/10, with odds ratio 1.71 [1.37, 2.13]. Correctness was assessed using task-specific unit tests, not unrestricted real-world software quality; time had a 40-minute cap, with 11/180 observations censored.

kp.k: Inline offers greatest efficiency on simple work
kp.d: On low-complexity Task A, Inline produced workload of 49.3 versus 56.0 for Chat and 58.1 for Structured, and completion time of 19.9 versus 24.5 and 25.1 minutes respectively. Correctness clustered around 8.3/10 without reliable between-mode differences after Holm correction. The authors interpret Inline's advantage as preserving editing flow and limiting interruptions on simple tasks, rather than delivering universally superior assistance.

kp.k: Chat improves correctness on more complex tasks
kp.d: On higher-complexity Task C, Chat achieved estimated correctness of 8.0/10, compared with Inline's 7.3 and Structured's 7.1, with reported p-values of 0.009 and 0.005 respectively. Chat and Inline completion times were comparable at 27.1 and 27.8 minutes; Structured took 29.7 minutes. Chat involved a median four prompt turns but only one compile–fail loop before a passing run, versus two for Inline and three for Structured. The authors interpret iterative clarification as containing error cascades.

kp.k: Structured assistance benefits novices under bounded conditions
kp.d: Among the 12 AI-cohort novices, Structured reduced Task B workload relative to Inline by 6.2 points [−10.7, −1.7] and improved correctness from 7.1/10 to 7.8/10, with odds ratio 1.37 [1.01, 1.86]. Experienced participants instead rated Structured as more effortful, with workload 5.0 points above Inline. The authors connect this pattern to expertise reversal: explicit requirements and checks can help less-experienced users while adding overhead for experts. The study's novice category still required 2–3 years of coding experience.

kp.k: Verification load captures checking and repair costs
kp.d: The authors introduce an equal-weight composite of compile/test failures, time-to-first-compile, normalized code churn, cumulative pauses exceeding two seconds and context switches. Components are standardized within task; higher scores indicate greater verification burden. Reported internal consistency was 0.80, and the first principal component explained 52.2% of variance. Failures and time-to-first-compile were the strongest reported predictors of subjective burden. The composite was added after preregistration using previously specified log variables, so it should be distinguished from preregistered primary outcomes.

kp.k: Immediate benefits coexist with rising fatigue
kp.d: Across tasks 1–3, adjusted fatigue increased by 0.70 KSS points [0.48, 0.92] in the AI cohort versus 0.48 [0.28, 0.68] in controls; the condition-by-index interaction had p=0.041. Stress increased numerically more with AI, by 0.17 versus 0.07 standardized SSSQ points, but the between-condition slope difference was not significant after multiplicity control, p=0.110. Within AI, reported mode-specific fatigue changes were +1.18 for Inline, +1.05 for Structured and +0.92 for Chat. These are short-session trajectories, not evidence of long-term occupational burnout.

kp.k: Verification statistically mediates some burden, without causal proof
kp.d: In the AI cohort, verification load statistically mediated approximately 26% of the task-index effect on fatigue and 24% on stress. Reported indirect effects were 0.15 [0.06, 0.27] for KSS and 0.08 [0.03, 0.16] for standardized SSSQ. The authors explicitly qualify the mechanism: verification load was observational, and significant indirect paths are consistent with checking and repair contributing to burden rather than establishing causation.

kp.k: Complexity thresholds and acceptance optima remain exploratory
kp.d: Johnson–Neyman analysis estimated that Chat surpassed Inline on correctness beyond approximately +0.40 standardized per-observation complexity, with crossover +0.41 [ +0.17, +0.64 ]. Structured's advantage occupied a narrower middle range, approximately −0.1 to +0.3. Because this complexity measure uses functions participants modified, it may itself be affected by interface mode and was treated as an exploratory moderator. Inline correctness also had an exploratory quadratic association with acceptance, peaking at 0.48 [0.44, 0.53]; this is not a validated instruction to accept half of all suggestions.

kp.k: Trust shocks can generate rejection and review fatigue
kp.d: The qualitative analysis of 60 interviews identified speed versus certainty, trust shocks, novice scaffolding and review fatigue. Participants described confident-looking errors as undermining trust and increasing checking or rejection. Action coding associated rejection streaks of at least five within three minutes and pause clusters with Inline-to-Chat switching, odds ratio 2.36 [1.33, 4.20], p=0.003. These reported associations contextualize the proposed verification mechanism rather than proving that switching reduces fatigue.

kp.k: Design recommendations target verification rather than output volume
kp.d: The authors recommend adaptive mode suggestions when failures, delayed compilation or pauses rise; optional Structured scaffolds for novices; local, on-demand rationales and uncertainty cues rather than continuous global confidence displays; and testable batches, runnable checks and sandboxes to shorten verification. They also recommend security co-review using static-analysis warnings and safer alternatives, drawing partly on cited security research. These are design implications and proposed deployment policies, not interventions experimentally validated in this study.

kp.k: Evaluation should include process burden and scope limits
kp.d: The authors recommend reporting verification load alongside workload, speed and correctness, comparing interfaces under backend parity and using equivalence tests when claiming practically unimportant differences. Generalization remains untested beyond three bounded Python tasks, one Structured design and predominantly single-session exposure. Tool-augmented backends, richer repository integration and long-term collaborative work may change effect sizes and crossovers. The small next-day follow-up was exploratory and underpowered; longitudinal and field studies are proposed rather than supplied.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Fan, Liu, Pan and Zhang claim that AI coding assistance improves immediate productivity and correctness, but leaves verification work that contributes to fatigue; the balance depends on interface, complexity and expertise.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about software development, not legal services. The authors report that pooled AI assistance reduced workload by 18.2 points on their four-subscale RAW–TLX composite, reduced completion time by 22% (25.0 versus 32.1 minutes), and improved test-based correctness (odds ratio 1.71; estimated scores 7.6 versus 6.2 out of 10). Holding GPT-4o fixed, Inline was fastest and lowest-load for simple work; Chat achieved higher correctness on complex work with comparable completion times; Structured prompting benefited novices at moderate complexity. Fatigue increased across tasks in both cohorts, with a greater increase under AI (KSS +0.70 versus +0.48; interaction p=0.041). The greater AI stress increase was numerical rather than statistically significant after correction (+0.17 versus +0.07; p=0.110). The authors associate checking and repair work with approximately 26% of the task-index effect on fatigue and 24% on stress, without claiming causal identification. They also report an exploratory association between Inline acceptance and correctness, peaking near 0.48 acceptance. Their proposed interventions—adaptive interface switching, on-demand transparency, testable suggestion packages and security co-review—are design recommendations rather than evaluated deployment outcomes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on a controlled mixed-methods study, instrumented behavioral measures, statistical models and participant interviews; mechanism and behavioral-threshold findings are qualified as exploratory or observational.
pts.d: The authors studied 60 professional software engineers and advanced computer-science students: 36 in a counterbalanced within-subject AI cohort and 24 in a randomized, matched no-AI cohort, yielding 180 task observations. Each participant completed three Python tasks covering parsing, authentication debugging and batch REST requests. All AI modes used GPT-4o version 2024-11-20 with fixed decoding. Workload, sleepiness and stress were measured by questionnaires; performance was measured through completion time and tests passed. Correctness scoring used a hidden immutable suite, supported by reference-implementation coverage and mutation checks. Mixed-effects models, multiplicity adjustments and reported sensitivity analyses support the outcome comparisons. The verification-load index combines failures, first-compile latency, churn, pauses and context switches; the authors report internal consistency of 0.80 and statistical mediation. The composite itself was added after preregistration, although its underlying log variables were preregistered. Complexity crossover and acceptance analyses were exploratory. Sixty interviews supplied qualitative context about flow, trust shocks, scaffolding and review fatigue. Recommendations additionally draw on cited research on cognitive load, interruptions, trust calibration and code security; the proposed adaptive policies were not experimentally tested here.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern short, supervised coding sessions with a fixed model and bounded tasks—not long-term adoption or autonomous software production.
pts.d: The 2026 paper reports three task blocks per participant, capped at 40 minutes each and separated by 15–20-minute breaks, plus an exploratory, underpowered next-day follow-up. No long-term productivity or workforce prediction is established. Backend parity involved fixed GPT-4o decoding, no tools or web access and task-level state resets. The authors limit generalization beyond these Python tasks, this Structured interface and the short exposure period; other languages, larger collaborative codebases and months-long use require testing. Richer integrations may change effect sizes and interface crossover points. The reported Chat-versus-Inline crossover around complexity z=+0.41 is relative to the study's standardized, per-observation metric, not a universal threshold. Because that metric depends on functions participants modified, the authors treat it as an exploratory moderator potentially influenced by treatment. The acceptance optimum near 0.48 is likewise descriptive, not a prescribed acceptance target. Mediation supports a possible verification-load mechanism rather than proving it. Comparable times on complex tasks should be distinguished from a universal claim that Chat never adds time.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Developers are affected differently by expertise and task complexity; interface designers and evaluators are urged to account for human checking costs alongside speed and quality.
pts.d: The direct participants were Python-proficient developers and advanced students with at least two years of programming experience. Thus, the study's novice group does not mean absolute programming beginners. Among AI participants, 12 were novices, 16 intermediate and eight experienced. Novices benefited from Structured prompting on moderate work: workload was 6.2 TLX points lower than Inline and correctness was 7.8 versus 7.1 out of 10. Experienced developers benefited from Inline on simple work and Chat on complex work, while Structured prompting imposed additional effort. Developers remained responsible for checking, editing and testing generated code: this is augmentation, not demonstrated replacement. Interviewees described trust loss after plausible errors and a desire to switch assistance styles after repeated rejections. For assistant designers, the authors recommend using failure loops, delayed compilation and pauses to trigger optional mode changes or verification support. For evaluators, they recommend reporting verification load alongside outcome measures. The paper makes no direct claims about lawyers, law firms, legal clients, legal markets or employment displacement.
